title: The axe meets the bow
hookLine: the older one hands over the stage, and stays a teacher
carry: parampara: handed on, teacher to student
tomorrow: Rama reaches the sea, and Sita is on the other side. now what?

lines: THE CAPTAIN HANDS OVER THE BAND.
cards: A senior captain hands the armband to a sophomore. A manager trains the person who'll replace her. There's an ache in that, and a strange pride.

On the road home from Rama's wedding, the sky darkens and a figure blocks the way: matted hair, an axe on one shoulder, a great bow on the other. It's Parashurama, and he's come to test the young prince.
By the end of the scene, he's the one who steps aside.

teach.b: In Valmiki's Ramayana, Parashurama has heard that Rama broke Shiva's great bow to win Sita. So he brings another bow, Vishnu's, and makes a challenge: string this one.
Rama takes the bow, strings it, and sets an arrow to it. And Parashurama sees who is standing in front of him. The fire drains out of him, and he knows this young prince is Vishnu himself.
So he yields. Rama's arrow is spent on the merit Parashurama had won, and Parashurama goes back to his mountain. Here's what's strange about that road.
Both of them are forms of Vishnu, and there they stand, face to face.
The older form steps aside for the younger, the man of the axe for the prince about to be tested by exile and war. And Parashurama doesn't vanish.
Tradition counts him among the chiranjivis, the long-lived ones, still at his practice on the mountain. In the Mahabharata he turns up again as a teacher of great warriors.
Hindus have a word for that chain: parampara. In the Gita, Krishna says his teaching came down that way, handed from one to the next.
It's why many Hindus honor their guru's guru, and why a grandmother shows a child how to light the lamp.
Stepping aside isn't disappearing. The axe passes the stage to the bow, and the teacher stays on.

how: Parashurama's meeting with Rama is told in Ramayana recitations and retold on stage in Ram Lila performances, where the man with the axe makes a dramatic entrance.

games.q: you've led the evening aarti at your temple's youth night for years. now a younger kid is taking over and doing it a bit differently. what fits Parashurama's road?
o: hand it on and stay to teach; that's how the parampara holds.
hand it on, but keep the final say on how it's done.
stay away completely, so they can't lean on you.
games.why: Parashurama yields the road to Rama, then teaches Bhishma, Drona and Karna in the Mahabharata. in a parampara, stepping aside isn't disappearing.

practice: Find one thing near you that someone older handed down or taught you to use: a lamp, a prayer, a recipe card, or a habit you can bring to mind. Hold it, or look at it, for the sit.
Let your breath slow, and think of who taught you, and who taught them. That's a parampara, and you're in it.

wordCard.voice: Parashurama: the sage's son with the axe, who met Rama on the road, saw Vishnu in him, stepped aside, and stayed a teacher.

orig.note: Sanskrit: long-lived. Tradition counts Parashurama among the chiranjivis, still at his practice.

carryVoice: The line: parampara, handed on from teacher to student. Parashurama gave Rama the road and stayed a teacher. Day fifteen fifty-two, complete.
